There is a particular hour, around three in the morning, when the parking lot behind a grocery store becomes its own tiny country. No one is left except the fluorescent lights humming their one low note, and the slow blink of a single security camera on the corner. The asphalt, still holding the day's heat, gives off a faint ghost of warmth through thin-soled shoes.

You stand there and realize the space is larger than it should be. The lines painted on the ground stretch into a kind of geometry feeling almost religious—rows and columns, the grid of human order laid bare in the dark. The vending machines glow from within like small chapels. A shopping cart wobbles in a nonexistent draft.

The silence is not empty. It is full of the particular quiet of a place that's stopped being used. The hum of the lights. The tick of metal cooling. A dog in the next building shifts on its crate. The whole scene feels provisional, as if the world reassembles around ten, snapping back to its louder shape.

And yet there is something in that suspended moment, the half-second between last and first, that asks you to simply be a body in a room. No name. No next appointment. Just the cold asphalt under your feet and the orange light of the exit sign, painting your hands in a color that isn't quite red.

You stand there for a long while, and the lot holds you without complaint.
